schema.source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
schema.description: {{COMPANY_NAME}} reusable Merlino Catalogue threat-profile template for System Integrator / MSP organisations. TP-08 models Internet-Facing Services Compromise across DNS/IP/software reconnaissance, active scanning, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, VPN/remote-service access, valid account abuse, web shell/server persistence, workload/token/secret theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, proxying and lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected disruptive impact. The profile is intentionally product-neutral and covers VPN, firewalls, web applications, APIs, project/support platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and cloud-hosted applications. Current Microsoft, CISA, Mandiant and MITRE campaign references provide threat-led evidence while product-specific CVEs remain dynamically enrichable. Organisation is represented by {{COMPANY_NAME}}.

data.Name: TP-08 | Gather Victim Network Information: DNS
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Enumerate corporate and customer-facing DNS records to identify VPN gateways, portals, APIs, project/support systems, mail services and administrative endpoints. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: DNS reveals the organisation's externally reachable service topology and can expose forgotten or business-unit-specific systems that are not consistently governed. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: External Reconnaissance. Primary assets at risk: Public DNS, VPN names, Support portals, Project portals, API endpoints, Admin portals. Detection opportunities: External attack-surface inventory; Passive DNS monitoring; Alert on unexpected new public records. Defensive considerations: Central DNS ownership; Remove stale records; Continuous attack-surface management.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: DNS reveals the organisation's externally reachable service topology and can expose forgotten or business-unit-specific systems that are not consistently governed. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Core; Phase=External Reconnaissance; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Identify public IP ranges and addresses associated with corporate offices, cloud services, VPN gateways, firewalls and exposed applications. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: IP-space knowledge enables focused scanning and can reveal direct-to-origin services that are not protected by expected CDN/WAF controls. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: External Reconnaissance. Primary assets at risk: Public IP addresses, Edge appliances, Cloud public IPs, Origin servers. Detection opportunities: External asset discovery; Unexpected public-IP exposure; Cloud public-IP inventory drift. Defensive considerations: Maintain authoritative external asset inventory; Remove unnecessary public IPs; Use private connectivity where possible.

data.Name: TP-08 | Gather Victim Host Information: Software
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Identify software and versions running on public services through banners, HTTP headers, TLS metadata, error pages, login portals and product-specific responses. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Version fingerprinting lets attackers match exposed products against known vulnerabilities and rapidly weaponize newly disclosed CVEs. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: External Reconnaissance. Primary assets at risk: VPN appliances, Firewalls, Jira/project portals, Service desks, Confluence, Web frameworks, Reverse proxies. Detection opportunities: Banner/version exposure review; ASM product fingerprinting; Unexpected legacy software. Defensive considerations: Suppress unnecessary version disclosure; Asset inventory; Rapid vulnerability management.

data.Name: TP-08 | Exploit Public-Facing Application
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Exploit a vulnerability or misconfiguration in an internet-facing application, firewall, VPN, project/support portal, API gateway or collaboration server to gain initial access. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is the defining ATT&CK technique for TP-08. Public-facing applications and edge devices are repeatedly exploited by ransomware, espionage and data-theft actors because they bypass user interaction and often sit at privileged network boundaries. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Initial Access. Primary assets at risk: VPN/SSL-VPN, Firewalls, Reverse proxies, Web applications, APIs, Confluence/Jira-like systems, Service desk/project portals. Detection opportunities: Exploit signatures; Unexpected child process from service; Web shell/file creation; New admin/session after exploit. Defensive considerations: KEV-driven patching; WAF/IPS; Exposure reduction; Segmentation; Virtual patching.

data.Name: TP-08 | External Remote Services
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Use legitimate VPN, Citrix, VNC, externally reachable remote management or other remote access services with compromised credentials. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: ATT&CK explicitly identifies VPN and other remote gateways as initial-access and persistence mechanisms. In a system-integrator environment these services often provide direct paths to administration networks. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Use Exposed Remote Access. Primary assets at risk: VPN, Citrix, VNC, Remote support gateways, Administrative access. Detection opportunities: Unusual login source/device; Access outside support hours; Successful login after failures. Defensive considerations: Phishing-resistant MFA; Named accounts; Device compliance; Source restrictions; No direct Tier-0 access.

Defensive considerations: Phishing-resistant MFA; Conditional Access; Least privilege; Risk-based session controls.

data.Description: Use compromised domain credentials through VPN, Citrix or other identity-integrated internet-facing remote access. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Remote-access gateways often authenticate against directory identities, turning a credential compromise into internal network access. Applicability: Hybrid / VPN. Internet-facing compromise phase: Use Domain-Backed VPN / Remote Account. Primary assets at risk: AD-integrated VPN, Citrix, Remote portals, Domain accounts. Detection opportunities: Domain account remote login from new device/location; Remote access followed by internal discovery. Defensive considerations: MFA; PAM/JIT; Separate remote-access groups; No standing admin remote login.

data.Name: TP-08 | Valid Accounts: Local Accounts
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Authenticate to an internet-facing appliance or application using a valid local administrator or service account. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Edge devices and legacy portals may retain local accounts outside central identity governance. Shared, default-like or stale accounts can provide high-impact access. Applicability: Edge / Appliance. Internet-facing compromise phase: Use Appliance / Local Admin Account. Primary assets at risk: Firewall admin, VPN local admin, Application local accounts, Appliance accounts. Detection opportunities: Local account login from new source; Use of dormant/stale account. Defensive considerations: Disable shared accounts; Vault credentials; MFA where supported; Periodic local-account review.

data.Name: TP-08 | Brute Force: Password Guessing
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Guess passwords against VPN, portals, administrative interfaces and web applications. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Internet-facing authentication services permit direct credential attacks, especially where MFA, throttling or lockout is weak. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Guess Exposed Service Password. Primary assets at risk: VPN, Admin portal, Web login, RMM portal. Detection opportunities: Repeated failures against one account; Low-and-slow guessing. Defensive considerations: MFA; Rate limiting; Smart lockout; Strong passwords.

data.Name: TP-08 | Brute Force: Password Spraying
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Attempt common passwords across many users on VPN, identity, SaaS and remote-access services. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Password spraying can identify a working enterprise identity without exploiting software and is especially relevant where email addresses are publicly discoverable. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Spray Internet-Facing Authentication. Primary assets at risk: VPN, Entra, SaaS, Remote services. Detection opportunities: Many users targeted from shared/distributed infrastructure; Authentication failure clustering. Defensive considerations: Phishing-resistant MFA; Smart lockout; Password protection.

data.Description: Reuse leaked or infostealer-derived credentials against exposed corporate services. data.Name: TP-08 | Steal Web Session Cookie
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Steal authenticated web-session material from a browser, proxy flow or compromised web service. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Session material can bypass fresh authentication and give immediate access to exposed portals or SaaS applications. Applicability: Web / SaaS. Internet-facing compromise phase: Steal Exposed Portal Session. Primary assets at risk: Web sessions, SaaS sessions, Admin portals. Detection opportunities: Session reuse from new device/IP; Concurrent impossible session use. Defensive considerations: Token/session protection; Managed devices; Rapid revocation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Steal Application Access Token
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Obtain OAuth, API or application tokens exposed by the compromised service, configuration, metadata or user session. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Internet-facing APIs and SaaS integrations often rely on bearer tokens; stolen tokens can provide direct programmatic access to internal or cloud resources. Detection opportunities: Token use from unusual client/IP; API calls after service exploitation. Defensive considerations: Short-lived tokens; Least privilege; Workload federation; Token rotation.

data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Replay a stolen session cookie to operate as an authenticated user or administrator. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Session replay can turn compromise of one browser or portal into valid-account access with reduced authentication friction. Applicability: Web / SaaS. Internet-facing compromise phase: Replay Stolen Portal Session. Primary assets at risk: Web portal, SaaS, Admin console. Detection opportunities: Session anomalies; New source for existing session. Defensive considerations: Session binding/token protection; Rapid revocation.

data.Description: Use cmd.exe or batch execution after exploiting an internet-facing Windows service. Defensive considerations: Central command/audit logs; Restrict shell access; Network isolation.

data.Description: Use Python for payload staging, proxying, enumeration or credential harvesting after server exploitation. Internet-facing compromise phase: Post-Exploit Execution. Primary assets at risk: Linux web servers, Application servers. Detection opportunities: Unexpected Python network access; Python launched by service process. Defensive considerations: Minimal server packages; EDR/auditd; Application control.

data.Name: TP-08 | Windows Management Instrumentation
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Use WMI for remote process execution after the attacker pivots from an exposed Windows server. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A public web-server foothold can become an internal administration foothold if the service account or harvested credentials reach other Windows systems. Applicability: Windows / Hybrid. Internet-facing compromise phase: Use WMI After Web Foothold. Primary assets at risk: Windows servers, Internal management. Detection opportunities: WmiPrvSE remote process creation; WMI from web server. Defensive considerations: Segmentation; Restrict WMI administration; EDR.

Inclusion rationale: A public web-server foothold can become an internal administration foothold if the service account or harvested credentials reach other Windows systems. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Description: Place a server-side script or executable that provides command execution through the compromised web service. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: ATT&CK defines web shells as persistent gateways into networks. They are a canonical post-exploitation technique for SharePoint, Exchange, web applications and collaboration servers. Applicability: Core Web Server. Internet-facing compromise phase: Persistence. Primary assets at risk: IIS, Apache/Nginx applications, SharePoint, Java web apps. Detection opportunities: New executable/script in webroot; Web process spawning shell; Rare POST requests to new file. Defensive considerations: FIM; WAF; EDR; Immutable deployment; Webroot permissions.

data.Name: TP-08 | Server Software Component: IIS Components
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Install or modify IIS modules/components to obtain durable execution in the web server process. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: IIS component persistence is harder to detect than a simple standalone web shell and may survive application-content replacement. Applicability: IIS Conditional. Internet-facing compromise phase: Persistence. Primary assets at risk: IIS, Windows web server. Detection opportunities: New IIS module/config; Unsigned module loaded into w3wp. Defensive considerations: IIS configuration integrity; Allow-list modules; EDR.

Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=IIS Conditional; Phase=Persistence; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. data.Name: TP-08 | Server Software Component: vSphere Installation Bundles
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Install a malicious or modified vSphere Installation Bundle on ESXi to obtain durable hypervisor-level persistence. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Where vCenter/ESXi administration is exposed or reachable from an edge compromise, hypervisor persistence creates exceptional blast radius and weak EDR visibility. Applicability: Virtualization Admin Exposure. Internet-facing compromise phase: Persist Through vSphere / ESXi Component. Primary assets at risk: ESXi, vSphere, Virtualization management. Detection opportunities: Unexpected VIB install; Acceptance-level changes; New hypervisor component. Defensive considerations: Isolate management plane; Signed components; Monitor VIB lifecycle.

data.Name: TP-08 | Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Create a scheduled task for backdoor, tunnel or payload execution. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Scheduled tasks provide simple persistence after a web or VPN foothold and can run under elevated service/admin accounts. Applicability: Windows. Internet-facing compromise phase: Persist on Windows Application Server. Primary assets at risk: Windows application server, Web server. data.Description: Create or modify a systemd service to run attacker code on boot. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Systemd provides durable persistence on Linux application servers and some general-purpose edge platforms. Applicability: Linux / Edge. Internet-facing compromise phase: Persist as Linux Service. Primary assets at risk: Linux web server, Application server. Detection opportunities: New systemd unit; Service binary outside approved path. Defensive considerations: FIM; auditd; Immutable build.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Systemd provides durable persistence on Linux application servers and some general-purpose edge platforms. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Linux / Edge; Phase=Persist as Linux Service; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Add an attacker-controlled SSH public key to a local or administrative account. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: SSH-key persistence can survive password changes and provide direct management access after the initial web or VPN exploit. Applicability: Linux / Edge. Internet-facing compromise phase: Add SSH Key to Exposed / Pivot Host. Primary assets at risk: Linux server, Appliance admin account, Jump host. Detection opportunities: authorized_keys modification; New SSH key after exploit. Defensive considerations: Short-lived SSH certificates; FIM; Restrict direct SSH.

data.Name: TP-08 | Create Account: Local Account
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Create a local user or admin account on the compromised service host or appliance. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Local persistence avoids dependence on the original exploit and may remain unnoticed on appliances outside normal identity governance. Applicability: Server / Appliance. Internet-facing compromise phase: Create Local Backdoor Account. Primary assets at risk: Local server account, Appliance admin. Detection opportunities: New account outside provisioning; Immediate admin assignment. Defensive considerations: Central account governance; Alert on local admin creation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Exploit a local vulnerability on the exposed server or appliance to elevate from the web/service account to root/SYSTEM/admin. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Public-facing services often run under restricted accounts; local privilege escalation unlocks credentials, persistence and internal network administration. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Exploit Local Privilege Vulnerability. Primary assets at risk: Web server, Application host, VPN appliance. Detection opportunities: Exploit chain after initial web process compromise; Kernel/service crash plus privilege change. Defensive considerations: Patch local vulnerabilities; Harden service accounts; Sandboxing.

data.Name: TP-08 | Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Sudo and Sudo Caching
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Use sudo permissions or cached sudo credentials to obtain root access. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Application administrators and appliance support accounts may have sudo paths that turn a service compromise into root control. Applicability: Linux / Edge. Internet-facing compromise phase: Elevate on Linux / Appliance. Primary assets at risk: Linux server, Edge appliance. Detection opportunities: Unexpected sudo from service account; sudoers abuse. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; No passwordless broad sudo; auditd.

data.Name: TP-08 | Exploitation for Credential Access
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Exploit a vulnerability specifically to obtain credentials, tokens or authentication material from the application, appliance or operating system. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Some edge and web vulnerabilities expose session databases, configuration or credential material even without full code execution. Applicability: Core / Conditional. Internet-facing compromise phase: Exploit Service to Extract Credentials. Primary assets at risk: VPN credentials, Session data, Application secrets. Detection opportunities: Unusual credential-store access following exploit; Exploit-specific telemetry. Defensive considerations: Patch KEVs; Credential isolation; Rotate secrets after appliance compromise.

This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Description: Read LSASS memory after elevating on an exposed Windows server. Detection opportunities: LSASS access; Credential-dumping detections. Defensive considerations: Credential Guard; No privileged interactive logon to web servers; EDR.

data.Name: TP-08 | OS Credential Dumping: Proc Filesystem
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Use /proc or process-memory access to recover tokens, passwords or secrets from Linux service processes. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Public web and application processes may hold database, API, SSO or cloud tokens in memory. Applicability: Linux. Internet-facing compromise phase: Read Linux Process Memory / Secrets. Primary assets at risk: Application process, Service tokens, Database credentials. Detection opportunities: Reads of /proc/<pid>/mem; ptrace by unexpected process. Defensive considerations: Process isolation; No secrets in long-lived environment; auditd.

This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Description: Steal private keys, certificates or SSH keys from the exposed server or appliance. data.Name: TP-08 | Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Query the instance metadata endpoint from a compromised cloud-hosted web application to obtain workload credentials. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A public cloud web-service exploit can immediately become cloud-control-plane compromise if the VM/container has an over-privileged managed identity. Applicability: Cloud / IaaS. Internet-facing compromise phase: Steal Managed Identity from Public Cloud Workload. Primary assets at risk: Managed identity, Cloud VM, Application workload. Detection opportunities: Unexpected IMDS access; Token use outside normal workload behavior. Defensive considerations: Least-privileged managed identities; Harden metadata access; Workload isolation.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: A public cloud web-service exploit can immediately become cloud-control-plane compromise if the VM/container has an over-privileged managed identity. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Cloud / IaaS; Phase=Steal Managed Identity from Public Cloud Workload; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Credentials from Password Stores: Password Managers
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Access password-manager data after pivoting to an admin/support endpoint. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A single password vault may expose many internal and customer systems. Applicability: Post-Pivot Conditional. Internet-facing compromise phase: Access Admin Password Vault. Primary assets at risk: Password manager, PAM vault. Detection opportunities: Vault export/new device access. Defensive considerations: Hardware-backed MFA; PAM; Restrict export.

data.Name: TP-08 | System Network Configuration Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Enumerate interfaces, routes, DNS and network configuration on the compromised public-facing system. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Edge and web servers often bridge public and internal networks; route information reveals management, application and database networks reachable from the foothold. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Map Internal Interfaces / Routes. Primary assets at risk: Internal routes, Management network, Application network. Detection opportunities: ipconfig/ifconfig/route after exploit. Defensive considerations: Segmentation; Minimal dual-homing; Behavioral detection.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Edge and web servers often bridge public and internal networks; route information reveals management, application and database networks reachable from the foothold. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Core; Phase=Map Internal Interfaces / Routes; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Windows / Linux; Phase=Enumerate Services; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Software Discovery: Security Software Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Identify endpoint, server or appliance security products. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Edge compromise is attractive partly because some devices have limited EDR support; where EDR exists, attackers may tailor their behavior to avoid or disable it. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Discover EDR / Security Tools. Primary assets at risk: EDR, AV, Host security. Detection opportunities: Security-software enumeration. Defensive considerations: Alert on discovery followed by tampering.

data.Name: TP-08 | Cloud Service Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Enumerate cloud services reachable through a compromised workload or stolen service identity. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A public cloud workload may have access to storage, databases, secrets, messaging or management services. Applicability: Cloud. Internet-facing compromise phase: Discover Cloud Services Available to Workload. Primary assets at risk: Azure services, Cloud storage, Databases, Secrets. Detection opportunities: Rapid service enumeration by workload identity. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; Behavior analytics.

data.Name: TP-08 | Cloud Service Dashboard
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Use legitimate dashboards after obtaining administrator or SaaS credentials. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Exposed service compromise may yield credentials that provide direct interactive access to cloud and application administration. Applicability: Cloud / SaaS. Internet-facing compromise phase: Inspect Cloud / SaaS Admin Dashboards. Primary assets at risk: Azure portal, SaaS admin, Project/service-desk admin. Detection opportunities: New portal/device/location after exploit. Defensive considerations: Conditional Access; PIM.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Exposed service compromise may yield credentials that provide direct interactive access to cloud and application administration. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Cloud / SaaS; Phase=Inspect Cloud / SaaS Admin Dashboards; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Cloud Infrastructure Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise

Defensive considerations: PIM; Least privilege.

data.Name: TP-08 | Cloud Storage Object Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: List files and objects in storage accessible to the public-facing application. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Internet-facing applications often hold direct data-store permissions, making object discovery an immediate post-exploit data-access route. Applicability: Cloud. Internet-facing compromise phase: Enumerate Cloud Storage Objects. Primary assets at risk: Object storage, Blobs, Application files, Backups. Detection opportunities: Mass listing after service compromise. Defensive considerations: Per-application storage scope; Monitor unusual enumeration.

data.Name: TP-08 | Remote Services: Cloud Services

data.Description: Use stolen cloud identities to move from the internet-facing workload into additional cloud and SaaS resources. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Cloud control planes can replace traditional network lateral movement when the public application already runs inside a cloud tenant. Applicability: Cloud. Internet-facing compromise phase: Pivot Through Cloud Control Plane. Primary assets at risk: Azure, M365, Cloud storage, SaaS. Detection opportunities: Cross-service access by workload/admin identity. Defensive considerations: PIM; Conditional Access; Least privilege.

Detection opportunities: Executable copied from DMZ/web server to internal host. Defensive considerations: Segmentation; EDR; File reputation.

Defensive considerations: Egress controls; NDR; Network segmentation.

data.Description: Use HTTP/HTTPS for backdoor communication, tunneling, payload download or data transfer. Detection opportunities: Non-browser HTTPS from service process; Rare destination; Periodic beacon. Defensive considerations: Egress allow-listing; Proxy/NDR; TLS/domain analytics.

data.Name: TP-08 | Web Service
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Use legitimate cloud/web services as command-and-control or dead-drop infrastructure. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Internet-facing hosts usually have broad web egress, making trusted web services effective camouflage. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Use Trusted Web Service for C2. Primary assets at risk: Cloud web services, Public repositories, Messaging services. Detection opportunities: Rare service use from server; Unexpected API patterns. Defensive considerations: Egress governance; Threat-intel enrichment.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Internet-facing hosts usually have broad web egress, making trusted web services effective camouflage. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Core; Phase=Use Trusted Web Service for C2; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Indicator Removal: File Deletion
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Delete staged tools, exploit files, logs or temporary data after use. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Public-service attackers often minimise disk evidence after establishing a more durable backdoor or proxy. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Delete Exploit / Web Shell Artifacts. Primary assets at risk: Temp files, Exploit payloads, Webroot artifacts. Detection opportunities: Rapid create-delete; Deletion after outbound transfer. Defensive considerations: Central logs; FIM; EDR.

data.Name: TP-08 | Disable or Modify System Firewall
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Disable or modify firewall rules to expose management services, allow C2 or enable lateral movement. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A compromised firewall/VPN appliance may itself be the enforcement point; altering its configuration can silently open new paths. Applicability: Core / Edge. Internet-facing compromise phase: Change Host / Appliance Firewall. Primary assets at risk: Host firewall, Edge firewall, VPN ACL. Detection opportunities: Firewall rule/config change from new admin/session; New external management rule. Defensive considerations: Config integrity; MFA; Change approval; Out-of-band config backup.

data.Description: Access SharePoint after recovering user, application or cloud tokens from the public-facing service. Detection opportunities: Bulk FileAccessed/FileDownloaded after service exploit. Defensive considerations: DLP; Least privilege; App permission governance.

This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Data from Cloud Storage
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Access objects and files in cloud storage using the application's managed identity, API keys or stolen user credentials. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Cloud-hosted applications often rely on object storage for uploads, documents and backups; excessive permissions can expose large datasets. Applicability: Cloud. Internet-facing compromise phase: Read Cloud Storage Used by Public Service. Primary assets at risk: Azure Storage, Object storage, Uploads, Backups. Detection opportunities: Mass object reads/downloads; New client using workload token. Defensive considerations: Per-app storage scope; Private endpoints; DLP; Versioning.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Cloud-hosted applications often rely on object storage for uploads, documents and backups; excessive permissions can expose large datasets. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Cloud; Phase=Read Cloud Storage Used by Public Service; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Data Destruction
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Delete application files, databases or cloud resources after obtaining sufficient privilege. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A public-facing compromise can become destructive if the attacker gains database, storage or cloud administration rights. Applicability: Destructive Follow-on. Internet-facing compromise phase: Destroy Public-Service / Backend Data. Primary assets at risk: Application data, Databases, Cloud resources. Detection opportunities: Mass delete; Database destructive operations; Cloud delete APIs. Defensive considerations: Immutable backups; Protected recovery; Resource locks.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: A public-facing compromise can become destructive if the attacker gains database, storage or cloud administration rights. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Destructive Follow-on; Phase=Destroy Public-Service / Backend Data; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Account Access Removal
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Disable or alter legitimate application, cloud or appliance administrator access. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Once high privilege is obtained, locking out defenders can prolong control of the compromised edge or application environment. Applicability: Admin Compromise. Internet-facing compromise phase: Lock Out Legitimate Admins. Primary assets at risk: Application admins, Cloud admins, Appliance admins. Detection opportunities: Admin disable/delete/password reset. Defensive considerations: Break-glass accounts; Out-of-band appliance recovery.
